content: Chorioamnionitis is an inflammatory condition that occurs during pregnancy and involves the uterus. It is caused by a bacterial infection of the amniotic sac and the surrounding amniotic fluid. This condition poses significant risks to both the mother and the fetus and is recognized as the most common cause of premature labor. Chorioamnionitis can be classified into subtypes based on the patient’s clinical presentation, the type of infiltrating immune cells, the anatomical regions affected by neutrophilic infiltration (stage), and the severity of inflammation (grade). The condition primarily affects the fetal membranes and is usually of infectious origin. A characteristic gross pathological finding in chorioamnionitis is the opaque appearance of the fetal membranes. Microscopically, the hallmark feature is neutrophilic infiltration of the amniotic cavity and/or the chorionic plate. The infection can be caused by bacterial, fungal, or viral microorganisms. It is essential to differentiate chorioamnionitis from other conditions that may present with similar symptoms, such as maternal fever, abdominal pain, or maternal/fetal tachycardia. For example, epidural-related fever should be considered in patients with epidural anesthesia who develop a low-grade fever without maternal or fetal tachycardia during labor. Extrauterine infections should be suspected in cases of fever and abdominal pain, while noninfectious conditions like placental abruption should be considered in patients with abdominal pain but no fever. Globally, the prevalence of chorioamnionitis is estimated to be approximately 4,000 cases per 100,000 individuals. It is more commonly observed in individuals under the age of 18. Gestational age is a significant predictor, with higher prevalence in pregnancies that end between 21 and 24 weeks of gestation. Male infants are more frequently affected than females, and the condition is more common among individuals of Hispanic and Asian/Pacific Islander descent. Several risk factors contribute to the development of chorioamnionitis. These include preterm premature rupture of membranes (PPROM), prematurity, nulliparity, prolonged labor, prolonged rupture of membranes, multiple digital vaginal examinations, meconium-stained amniotic fluid, internal fetal monitoring, epidural anesthesia, maternal immunocompromised states, certain maternal behavioral conditions, and infections. Clinically, chorioamnionitis is associated with maternal fever, uterine tenderness, purulent or foul-smelling amniotic fluid, and maternal or fetal tachycardia. Fetal complications include preterm birth, neonatal sepsis, neurological complications, and respiratory issues. Maternal complications may include sepsis, infections, and labor-related complications such as cesarean delivery or postpartum hemorrhage. There is no single definitive diagnostic test for chorioamnionitis. Diagnosis is typically based on clinical presentation, laboratory findings, and/or histopathological evaluation. Clinical chorioamnionitis is diagnosed based on features such as maternal fever, uterine tenderness, maternal or fetal tachycardia, and foul-smelling or purulent amniotic fluid. The gold standard for diagnosis is a microbiological culture of the amniotic fluid. On physical examination, findings may include fever, abdominal pain, uterine tenderness, tachycardia, and foul-smelling vaginal discharge. Laboratory findings consistent with chorioamnionitis include maternal leukocytosis, a left shift or elevated band count, and specific findings in the amniotic fluid, such as positive microbiological culture results, the presence of bacteria or white blood cells on Gram stain, decreased glucose levels, and elevated interleukin-6 (IL-6) levels. Histological findings include neutrophilic infiltration of the chorioamniotic membranes. There are no specific findings on electrocardiogram (ECG), X-ray, or ultrasound directly associated with chorioamnionitis. However, ultrasound may be useful in identifying complications such as postpartum hemorrhage, pelvic abscesses, endomyometritis, intraventricular hemorrhage, periventricular leukomalacia, respiratory distress syndrome, and bronchopulmonary dysplasia. Similarly, CT scans and MRIs do not show direct findings of chorioamnionitis but may help diagnose complications such as pelvic infections, abscesses, spontaneous preterm delivery, white matter injury, and intraventricular hemorrhage. Magnetic resonance spectroscopy (MRS) may detect neuroinflammation and predict poor neurodevelopmental outcomes, such as motor or cognitive impairments, in affected infants. The primary treatment for chorioamnionitis is antimicrobial therapy. The preferred regimen is a combination of ampicillin and gentamicin. Supportive therapies, such as antipyretics, may also be administered. Surgical intervention is not recommended for managing this condition. Primary prevention strategies include inducing labor after 34 weeks of gestation and administering prophylactic antimicrobial therapy in cases of preterm premature rupture of membranes (PPROM).
